meta.title: Who really said "I know that I know nothing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Socrates never said it in these words. The line occurs nowhere in Plato; it's a compression of Apology 21d, "I neither know nor think that I know."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I know that I know nothing'?
meta.ogDescription: The famous line appears nowhere in Plato. It's a later paraphrase of Apology 21d, routed through Cicero's Latin and back-translated into Greek.

answer.label: Not Socrates — a later paraphrase
answer.authorDates: c. 470–399 BC · Athenian philosopher, tried and executed in Athens
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Socratic, but the wording is not his. The line “I know that I know nothing” occurs nowhere in Plato’s works in precisely that form. It is a compressed paraphrase of Apology 21d, where Jowett’s translation reads “I neither know nor think that I know” — a claim about not overestimating his knowledge, not a boast of certain ignorance.
answer.confidenceText: The idea is Socrates’. The sentence is somebody else’s.

source.heading: The nearest real text

docMeta.dd: 21d — Socrates recounts examining a politician reputed to be wise

source.excerpt: Well, although I do not suppose that either of us knows anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is,—for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.
trail: Plato, Apology 21d (4th c. BC). The genuine sentence. Jowett’s translation reads “I neither know nor think that I know”; Harold North Fowler’s renders the same passage “I, as I do not know anything, do not think I do either” (Perseus Digital Library ↗). Neither is the slogan.

Cicero, Academica, Book I, section 16 (45 BC). The Latin route. Cicero writes that Socrates “nihil se scire dicat nisi id ipsum … ipse se nihil scire id unum sciat” — but the neat tag “scio me nihil scire” does not appear in the Latin text itself (The Latin Library ↗). Even the Latin famously attached to this quote is a summary of Cicero, not a line from him.

Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers II.32 (3rd c. AD). R. D. Hicks’ translation reports that Socrates “knew nothing except just the fact of his ignorance” — a doxographer’s summary written some six centuries after Socrates died (Wikisource ↗).

The modern verdict. Wikiquote lists this phrasing under Misattributed, deferring to Wikipedia’s dedicated article, which states the saying “actually occurs nowhere in Plato’s works in precisely the form” quoted (Wikipedia ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the passage the slogan is squeezed out of. Note what Socrates actually claims: not that he knows he knows nothing, but that he does not imagine he knows what he does not. The difference is the whole point — and it is exactly what the popular version destroys.

sourceLink.text: Plato, Apology, translated by Benjamin Jowett (Project Gutenberg)

source.rightsNote: The excerpt shown is Benjamin Jowett’s 19th-century English translation of the Apology — Jowett died in 1893, and the text is distributed as public domain by Project Gutenberg ↗, so both the Greek original and this rendering are free of copyright in the United States. Note that other translations of the same passage are not: a modern rendering of an ancient text carries its own fresh copyright, so quoting Apology 21d from a recent edition is a different rights question entirely. The popular slogan itself has no identifiable author to hold a claim in it.

author.name: Socrates
author.kicker: The true author of the thought
author.heading: The man who wrote none of it down
author.bio: Socrates left no writings of his own. Everything credited to him reaches us through other people — chiefly Plato and Xenophon, later Diogenes Laërtius, and in Latin, Cicero. That is precisely why quotations “by Socrates” are so slippery: every one of them is already a report, and often a translation of a report. His actual position in the Apology is subtler than the slogan — he claims to be wiser than others only in that he does not imagine he knows what he does not know.

misattribution.heading: How a hedge became a slogan
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication invented from nothing — it is something subtler and more common: a real philosophical position, flattened by centuries of translation and re-translation into a sentence its subject never uttered. Four things go wrong at once.

items.why: Wikipedia’s dedicated article is blunt: the saying, “though widely attributed to Plato’s Socrates in both ancient and modern times, actually occurs nowhere in Plato’s works in precisely the form” quoted. Wikiquote accordingly files it under Misattributed (Wikiquote, Socrates ↗).

Cicero’s Academica I.16 does describe Socrates as one who “ipse se nihil scire id unum sciat” — but reading the Latin text itself, the crisp motto “scio me nihil scire” is nowhere in it (The Latin Library ↗). The tag is a summary of Cicero that later acquired his authority.

items.scope: The Greek “ἓν οἶδα ὅτι οὐδὲν οἶδα”
items.why: The Greek version people cite as the authentic source runs the wrong way down the chain. Wikipedia records that it “was later back-translated to Katharevousa Greek” — i.e. it is a modern Greek rendering of the Latin, not the ancient Greek of Plato (Wikipedia ↗).

The slogan makes Socrates a total sceptic. He was not. Evidence that he does not claim to know nothing sits a few pages later at Apology 29b–c, “where he claims twice to know something” — and at 29d he is confident enough in that knowledge to die for it (Wikipedia ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: What Socrates actually said, as far as any text records it, is a careful double negative: “I neither know nor think that I know” (Apology 21d, trans. Jowett ↗). He is not claiming knowledge of his own ignorance — he is declining to claim anything at all. The popular version hands him back exactly the certainty he spent his life refusing.

context.heading: Why the difference matters
lead: Socrates wrote nothing. Every sentence we have from him is already someone else’s report, and usually a translation of one — which makes him uniquely vulnerable to this kind of drift. Here the drift ran Greek → Latin (Cicero’s paraphrase) → a tidy Latin motto nobody actually wrote → English → and then back into modern Greek, where it now poses as the original. Each step lost a qualification.

The qualification was the point. In the Apology, Socrates is explaining why the Delphic oracle called him the wisest man: not because he possesses some special knowledge of his own ignorance, but because, unlike the men he cross-examined, he does not pretend. His wisdom is negative — an absence of false confidence, not a possession. “I know that I know nothing” converts that absence into a trophy, which is precisely the move he was mocking.
detailsBody: Read literally, “I know that I know nothing” is self-refuting: if you know that, you know something. Generations of readers have treated this as a deep Socratic paradox — and it is discussed as such all over the internet. But the paradox is an artefact of the translation chain, not of Socrates. His actual formulation at 21d has no such problem, because he never asserts knowledge of his ignorance in the first place; he simply reports that he does not think he knows what he does not know.
This is the tell of a paraphrase that has travelled too far: it generates a philosophical puzzle that vanishes the moment you open the primary text.
context.pull: He is not claiming to know his own ignorance. He is declining to claim anything at all.
